Please polish the following text to make it more eloquent and professional, keeping all original information unchanged:

LONGMONT, Colorado (CNN) -- A Colorado solar-energy company has high hopes for the economic stimulus bill that President Barack Obama will sign Tuesday in Denver. AVA Solar CEO Pascal Noronha holds one of the solar panels his company produces. Obama touts that the stimulus bill will help create up to a half a million so-called "green" jobs in the field of alternative energy. Colorado has a growing green energy industry. Executives of AVA Solar, based in Fort Collins, Colorado, are among green energy industry representatives invited to the bill signing. AVA Solar has its plant in Longmont, about 30 minutes north of Denver. The plant, set to begin production in the spring, will construct solar panels for solar power plants. Once production is up to speed, CEO Pascal Noronha says, the plant should create enough solar panels a year to power 40,000 U.S. homes. Noronha says AVA Solar needs two things: Government loans to expand its factory, and more government assistance to help power companies commit to building large solar power plants in the United States. iReport.com: What would you fix first? Noronha says those two moves would help AVA Solar create 1,000 to 2,000 new jobs in its factory, plus added employment for its suppliers. The company, founded in 2007, currently has 175 employees. Without the stimulus, Noronha said, AVA Solar is on track to create 420 new jobs by the end of this year. AVA Solar currently operates on $175 million in U.S.-based private venture capital. In 2007 the company also received $3 million in seed money from the U.S. Department of Energy. Noronha says Obama is on the right track in terms of the stimulus bill. "What everybody needs is a little seed money because five years from now there's no question [that] solar has to replace the oil that we import," Noronha says. "What the government needs to do is provide the traction that is needed to get the first few projects on the ground." "We need money from the federal government ... to facilitate production immediately," the CEO adds. "Otherwise, we will be sitting and waiting for projects in the U.S., and if we have to wait one year or two years -- when we're able to produce a solution for this country today -- that is a really good reason for the government to say, 'Here it is, let's go.' " Noronha says his company's biggest customer base is in Germany, a country that is far ahead of the United States in embracing solar energy. Obtaining U.S. customers is a priority, he explains. "As a company we would very much like to have customers here in the U.S.," Noronha says. "The government needs to be able to facilitate these customers by making it possible for them to put large-scale power plants up." Noronha is optimistic about the stimulus bill and the direction of the Obama administration. "If you look at the vision of the president, you know he is looking out in the future and saying we've got to reduce our dependence on foreign oil," Noronha says. "Well, to reduce our dependence on foreign oil, there is only renewable energy. And there are two forms that are promising -- one is wind and the other is solar. And solar, you've got the sun's resources all over the world."

LONGMONT, Colorado (CNN) — AVA Solar, a Colorado-based solar-power business, is anticipating major benefits from the economic recovery legislation President Barack Obama is scheduled to sign Tuesday in Denver.

Obama has said the measure could generate as many as 500,000 alternative-energy positions, often described as “green” jobs. Colorado’s clean-energy sector is already expanding, and AVA Solar executives are among the industry representatives invited to attend the signing ceremony.

The company is headquartered in Fort Collins, Colorado, while its manufacturing facility is located in Longmont, roughly a 30-minute drive north of Denver. Production is expected to start in the spring. The factory will make panels intended for solar power stations. According to CEO Pascal Noronha, once the operation reaches full capacity, it should manufacture enough panels annually to supply electricity to 40,000 American households. Noronha has been photographed holding one of the panels produced by the company.

He says AVA Solar requires two forms of federal support: government-backed financing to enlarge its manufacturing facility and additional assistance that would encourage utility companies to move forward with large solar-plant projects in the United States.

iReport.com asks: What would you repair first?

Noronha estimates that these two steps could allow AVA Solar to add between 1,000 and 2,000 factory jobs, while also creating further employment among its suppliers. Established in 2007, the company currently employs 175 people. Even without money from the stimulus package, it expects to add 420 positions by the end of this year.

AVA Solar is funded by $175 million in private venture capital from U.S. sources. It also obtained $3 million in initial funding from the U.S. Department of Energy in 2007.

Noronha believes Obama’s stimulus approach is moving in the proper direction. In his view, companies need a modest amount of startup funding because solar power will inevitably have to replace imported petroleum within five years. He says the government should create enough momentum to launch the first several projects.

The CEO also argues that immediate federal financing is necessary to accelerate manufacturing. Otherwise, he says, the company could spend one or two years waiting for American projects even though it is already capable of offering the country a solution. That, he believes, is a strong justification for the government to provide funding and authorize work to begin.

Germany, which has adopted solar power much more extensively than the United States, currently represents AVA Solar’s largest customer market. Noronha says securing buyers in the United States is a key objective. The company would strongly prefer to serve domestic customers, he explains, but federal action is needed to help those customers develop utility-scale solar facilities.

Noronha remains positive about both the stimulus legislation and the Obama administration’s broader strategy. He says the president’s long-term goal is to decrease U.S. reliance on overseas oil. Achieving that objective, Noronha argues, requires renewable power. He identifies wind and solar as the two most promising options, noting that sunlight is available throughout the world.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a CNN-style news article about Colorado solar company AVA Solar’s expectations for President Obama’s 2009 economic stimulus bill and its potential to create green jobs.
counterfactuals.output:
# Colorado solar manufacturer looks to stimulus plan for green-job growth

**LONGMONT, Colorado (CNN)** — For AVA Solar, President Barack Obama’s 2009 economic stimulus package offered more than a boost for renewable energy. The Colorado company hoped it would help turn a young solar-panel business into a source of large-scale manufacturing jobs.

AVA Solar, later renamed Abound Solar, was developing thin-film photovoltaic modules at a factory in Longmont. Its technology used semiconductor material deposited on glass, an approach intended to reduce costs and make solar power more competitive with electricity generated from fossil fuels.

The company expected the American Recovery and Reinvestment Act to increase demand for its products while making it easier to finance new factories and production lines. The $787 billion stimulus law included tens of billions of dollars for clean energy, including renewable-power projects, efficiency programs, loan guarantees and tax incentives for advanced-energy manufacturing.

For companies such as AVA Solar, those provisions held the potential to address two challenges at once: limited access to capital during the recession and weak demand for new energy projects.

Federal support could encourage utilities, businesses and developers to move forward with solar installations that might otherwise be delayed. Manufacturing incentives and loan programs could also help domestic producers expand without relying entirely on private credit markets, which tightened sharply during the financial crisis.

That expansion, company supporters argued, could create jobs ranging from engineers and laboratory researchers to factory technicians, electricians and construction workers. It could also generate work among equipment suppliers and other businesses serving a growing solar industry.

Colorado officials were promoting renewable energy as an important part of the state’s economic future. With research institutions, skilled workers and an emerging clean-technology sector, the state was competing to become a center for what Obama frequently described as the “green economy.”

But stimulus money alone offered no guarantee of success. Solar manufacturers faced competition from larger overseas producers, changing panel prices and continued uncertainty in financial markets. Thin-film companies also had to prove that they could increase production while maintaining quality and lowering costs.

The broader question was how quickly federal incentives would translate into actual projects and hiring. Much depended on how agencies implemented the programs, whether developers could obtain financing and whether demand for solar power continued after the temporary stimulus measures expired.

Still, AVA Solar represented the type of company the administration hoped to encourage: a domestic manufacturer attempting to commercialize new energy technology while creating jobs in a recession-battered economy.

For Colorado, the promise was that clean-energy spending would do more than install solar panels. It could help build the factories—and the workforce—that produced them.
counterfactuals.label: cf_1

counterfactuals.prompt: Report on how the federal stimulus package could help AVA Solar expand its Longmont factory, secure U.S. customers, and increase solar-panel production.
counterfactuals.output:
## How the federal stimulus could help AVA Solar

The 2009 American Recovery and Reinvestment Act could support AVA Solar—later renamed Abound Solar—on both the manufacturing and customer sides of its business.

### Expand the Longmont factory

AVA Solar’s Longmont, Colorado, plant was designed to manufacture low-cost cadmium-telluride thin-film photovoltaic modules, with production expected to scale toward roughly 200 megawatts annually. Stimulus provisions could help finance that expansion through:

- **Department of Energy loan guarantees**, reducing the risk and borrowing cost of buying production equipment and adding manufacturing lines.
- **The Section 48C manufacturing tax credit**, which covered up to 30% of qualifying investments in factories producing renewable-energy equipment.
- **Grants, accelerated depreciation, and related incentives** that could lower the cash required for construction and equipment.
- **Federal and state clean-energy spending**, which could improve access to capital and support hiring as the plant ramped up.

These measures were particularly important because the financial crisis had made conventional loans and private investment harder to obtain.

### Help secure U.S. customers

At the time, much of the strongest solar demand was overseas, especially in subsidized European markets. U.S. developers often had difficulty financing projects because the “tax-equity” market had contracted.

The stimulus addressed that problem by allowing eligible renewable-energy projects to receive a **cash grant equal to 30% of project cost in place of the federal investment tax credit**. It also extended solar tax incentives and funded solar installations on federal, state, municipal, military, and public-building properties.

That could make projects using AVA panels more affordable and bankable, giving the company:

- A stronger domestic sales pipeline.
- Opportunities to supply government and utility-scale projects.
- Less dependence on European customers.
- Greater credibility with project developers seeking a U.S.-made module supplier.

### Increase production and employment

With factory financing and customer demand improving at the same time, AVA could operate its Longmont lines at higher utilization, lower per-panel costs through scale, and hire additional workers. Higher volume was central to its plan to make thin-film modules competitive with conventional crystalline-silicon panels.

### Important limitation

The stimulus did not guarantee AVA’s success. Tax credits and grants generally required qualifying investments or completed projects, while loan guarantees still involved federal review and commercial risk. AVA, as Abound Solar, later received a federal loan guarantee but ultimately ceased operations in 2012. Nevertheless, when the stimulus was enacted, its combination of manufacturing assistance, project finance, and government clean-energy spending offered a plausible route to expanding the Longmont factory and building a U.S. customer base.
counterfactuals.label: cf_2

counterfactuals.prompt: Create a news story based on an interview with AVA Solar CEO Pascal Noronha about government loans, renewable-energy investment, job creation, and reducing dependence on foreign oil.
counterfactuals.output:
### AVA Solar CEO Says Government Loans Can Spur Clean-Energy Jobs, Cut Oil Dependence

Government-backed loans can help renewable-energy companies expand manufacturing, create jobs and strengthen U.S. energy security, AVA Solar CEO Pascal Noronha said in an interview.

Noronha said access to capital remains one of the biggest challenges for companies seeking to bring renewable-energy technologies to commercial scale. Government loan programs can encourage private investment by reducing the risks associated with building factories and deploying new technologies, he said.

The support is not simply a subsidy for individual companies, Noronha argued, but an investment in a domestic clean-energy industry. Financing renewable-energy projects can generate construction and manufacturing jobs while supporting broader supply chains and local economies.

Noronha also linked renewable-energy investment to the country’s dependence on foreign oil. Expanding domestic sources of power would diversify the nation’s energy supply and keep more energy spending within the United States, he said.

Critics of government lending programs have raised concerns about taxpayer exposure and the government’s role in selecting companies for support. Noronha said such programs should include careful review and accountability, while recognizing that emerging energy industries often require significant upfront investment.

He added that consistent federal policy is important for attracting private capital. Clear, long-term incentives would give investors greater confidence and help U.S. companies compete with foreign manufacturers that may receive substantial backing from their own governments.

For AVA Solar, the broader goal is to turn renewable energy into a source of industrial growth as well as environmental progress. Noronha said government loans, combined with private investment, could accelerate that transition, create domestic jobs and reduce the economic and strategic risks associated with reliance on imported oil.
counterfactuals.label: cf_3

counterfactuals.prompt: Explain how Obama’s stimulus bill might affect Colorado’s growing green-energy industry, using AVA Solar as the main example and including relevant employment and funding figures.
counterfactuals.output:
Obama’s 2009 stimulus could accelerate Colorado’s green-energy sector by lowering the cost of building factories and renewable projects, expanding federal loan guarantees and tax credits, and creating demand through government energy-efficiency and clean-power spending.

AVA Solar—later renamed Abound Solar—illustrated the potential. The Fort Collins–area company was commercializing thin-film solar panels and building a manufacturing plant near Loveland. At the time, it employed roughly 100–150 people; the new plant was expected to support about 200 jobs initially and potentially grow to around 500 workers as production expanded. Access to a federal loan guarantee—reportedly on the order of $100 million—could help AVA buy equipment, enlarge the factory and hire more workers more quickly.

More broadly, the roughly $787 billion recovery act contained about $70–80 billion for clean energy, efficiency and related tax incentives. Colorado was eligible for approximately:

- **$79.5 million** for home weatherization,
- **$49.2 million** through the State Energy Program, and
- **about $40 million** in local energy-efficiency block grants.

That spending would not all go directly to AVA Solar, but it could stimulate orders for solar equipment, attract private investment and create jobs among Colorado manufacturers, installers and suppliers. The main uncertainty was whether the money would reach projects quickly enough—and whether demand would remain strong after the temporary federal support ended.
counterfactuals.label: cf_4

# AVA Solar looks to expand as Obama signs stimulus bill in Denver

**DENVER (CNN)** — Executives from Colorado-based AVA Solar were among the business leaders attending President Barack Obama’s signing of the $787 billion economic stimulus package in Denver, an event intended to highlight the administration’s push to create jobs through clean-energy investment.

The company, which produces thin-film photovoltaic modules for large solar installations, is preparing to expand its manufacturing capacity as demand for renewable energy grows. AVA Solar’s plans call for increased production and additional hiring in Colorado, positioning the company to supply utility-scale projects rather than primarily serving the residential rooftop market.

Chief executive Pascal Noronha said federal support is critical because large solar developments require substantial capital and can take years to finance, permit and build. Tax incentives, grants, loan guarantees and investment in transmission infrastructure could help reduce the risks facing developers and manufacturers, he argued.

Noronha’s case reflects a broader concern in the renewable-energy industry: Even when solar technology is ready for commercial deployment, projects can stall because financing is unavailable or electricity cannot easily be moved from sunny, remote areas to population centers.

The stimulus legislation includes billions of dollars for renewable energy, efficiency improvements and modernization of the nation’s electric grid. The Obama administration says those investments will create jobs in the near term while helping the United States reduce its dependence on fossil fuels.

For AVA Solar, the measure could strengthen the market for the large installations its technology is designed to serve. The company uses a manufacturing process intended to lower the cost of producing solar modules, an approach that could make solar power more competitive with conventional electricity as production increases.

Noronha said the industry’s long-term goal should be to compete without permanent government assistance. But he maintained that federal action is needed now to help companies scale up factories, attract private investment and bring major projects online.

Obama signed the bill at the Denver Museum of Nature & Science, choosing Colorado in part because of the state’s growing clean-energy sector. The setting allowed the administration to present renewable energy as both an environmental priority and a potential source of manufacturing and construction jobs.

AVA Solar’s expansion will still depend on execution, market demand and access to capital. But company officials see the stimulus package as an opportunity to accelerate projects that might otherwise be delayed by the economic downturn and tight credit markets.
counterfactuals.label: cf_5
